conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Smith. I'm Dr. Lee. I understand the nursing home had trouble replacing your catheter today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… hard to pass. Thirsty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’re not having pain with urination, fever, or back pain, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just thirsty. Leg hurts like always.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. The urology team was able to place a new hydrogel catheter in the ER. It went in fine, and we saw clear yellow urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good… glad it’s in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did some urine and blood tests. The urine showed signs of bacteria and white blood cells, which can happen with long-term catheters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. You don’t have a fever or symptoms, and your white blood cell count, while a bit high, is similar to your last hospital stay. It may not be a true infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So… no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You got one dose in the ER just in case. But since you’re not sick and your labs are stable, we’re stopping antibiotics. We’re sending cultures to check, but they’ll come back after you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat blood work looks better. White count dropped to normal. That supports our decision not to continue antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Still thirsty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you fluids through your GJ tube. Your blood sugar is stable, so we’ll restart your regular tube feeds today at the nursing home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your regular medications are continuing—gabapentin, fentanyl patch, morphine as needed. Nothing has changed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re clearing you to go back to the nursing home. The catheter is working, labs improved, and you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The urine and blood cultures are still pending, but we don’t expect them to change anything. Your team at the home will watch for any fever or issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Just want to get back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your home team knows everything—meds, feeds, and the catheter change. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How’s the leg pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same. Usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your pain plan the same. Use the morphine as needed through the GJ tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks, Doctor.
